data.title: Investors are betting on U.S. Treasuries as yields rise
data.description:
Investors are increasingly betting on more upside in U.S. Treasuries, according to analysts at The Kobeissi Letter.

The extra cost investors are willing to pay for call options on longer-dated Treasuries (US30Y), (US20Y), (US10Y) relative to puts has climbed to approximately 50 basis points—the highest level since March 2025.

 

 

This marks a sharp reversal from a 250-basis-point premium for puts over calls in late September, The Kobeissi Letter noted.

Treasury prices have been gaining as yields decline. The 10-Year Note Yield (US10Y) has fallen below 5.00% for the first time since Sept. 23, now down 40 basis points from its Oct. 7 peak.

This suggests investors are increasingly betting on further gains in Treasury prices," the analysts wrote.

The Kobeissi Letter highlighted that one notable options trade is targeting a drop in the 10-Year Note Yield to approximately 4.60% within a month, involving roughly 65,000 contracts and costing around $7 million in premium.

"The bond market is seeing massive swings in price and sentiment," the analysts observed.

data.title: Smith & Nephew was in discussions to merge with J&J unit, talks collapsed - FT
data.description:
Smith & Nephew (SNN) was in advanced discussions to combine with Johnson & Johnson’s (JNJ) orthopedics business, though a deal fell apart over who would run the enlarged company.

Smith & Nephew (SNN) refused to agree to the combined group being led by its former chief executive Namal Nawana, who left in 2019, according to a  Financial Times report earlier on Friday, which cited people familiar with the matter. JNJ wanted to put Nawana, the head of its orthopedics unit, as the merged company's new chief.

Smith & Nephew Chair Rupert Soames, who would have continued to lead the board, made the demand a “red line” in talks, according to the report. The companies were targeting a mid-October announcement before talks shuttered several weeks ago.

The two companies had agreed that JNJ holders would own 50.1% of the combined company, with Smith & Nephew shareholders owning the rest, according to the report. Smith & Nephew would have paid J&J a dividend of $10 billion to account for the discrepancy in valuations by raising debt.

UK-listed Smith & Nephew (SNN) approached JNJ earlier this year with its offer to combine with JNJ's orthopedics unit, the FT reported. The proposed deal valued the hip and knee replacement unit at as much as $22 billion—almost double Smith & Nephew’s £9.4bn ($12.6bn) market cap.

J&J and Smith & Nephew declined to comment to the FT.

J&J (JNJ) announced plans last October to separate its orthopedics business, which reportedly has attracted interest from several private equity firms. Earlier this month, JNJ Chief Financial Officer Joseph Wolk told the WSJ that the company was “leaning” toward spinning out the unit.

“We think the best value creation at this moment in time for J&J shareholders is to spin it straight out,” Wolk said in an interview with the WSJ.

Last month there were media reports that Apollo Global Management (APO) was in talks to acquire ‌Johnson & Johnson's (JNJ) DePuy Synthes orthopedics unit in a deal that could value it at close ​to $20 billion.

data.title: Infosys signals 1%-2% FY27 constant-currency growth as AI revenue reaches 10.5% and large deals hit $5.2B
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Infosys (INFY) Q2 FY2027

Management View

  • CEO Salil Parekh said Q2 constant-currency revenue growth was modest while AI and large deals were the standout: "Our revenue growth for Q2 was at 1.5% year-on-year and 1.2% sequentially in constant currency terms." He added: "Our AI revenue was standout at ... of our total revenue, growing 29% sequentially. Last quarter, it was at 8.2%."

  • Parekh highlighted deal momentum and called out two mega deals, including a net-new multi-year award: "Our large deals were another standout at $5.2 billion for the quarter. This includes 2 mega deals." He said one was "over $2 billion ... for a period of 7 years, and it's net new" and "expected to contribute over 1% of revenue growth in the coming financial year," while "The second mega deal was for $1 billion for a renewal."

  • CFO Jayesh Sanghrajka framed the quarter as below internal expectations on growth, with AI mix increasing and competitive pricing pressure: "Client spending remains cautious" and "revenue growth was below our expectations." He said, "Q2 revenues were $5,145 million" and added that "volumes were softer and price increases were lower than anticipated amidst high competitive intensity."

Outlook

  • Management revised FY2027 constant-currency revenue growth guidance to "1% to 2% year-on-year," while keeping profitability targets unchanged: "Our operating margin guidance remains the same at 20% to 22%," Parekh said.

  • Sanghrajka attributed the guidance change to factors including pricing and discretionary demand, saying pricing expansion expected earlier "has not materialized" due to "competitive intensity," alongside "softer-than-expected revenue growth" and "slower discretionary spend" in "retail and High Tech."

  • Entering the second half, Sanghrajka cautioned on seasonality: "we are entering the seasonally weaker part of the year" with "furloughs" and "lower working days." He added: "At this point in time, we can't really say where we will end up."

Financial Results

  • Revenue was $5,145 million vs. analysts’ revenue estimate $5,180,564,814.42 (FY2027 Q2).

  • Sanghrajka said free cash flow was "$928 million" and EPS was "INR 19.32." He also stated, "We ended the quarter with cash and cash equivalents at $4.7 billion and a debt-free balance sheet."

  • On profitability, Sanghrajka said, "Q2 operating margins were a 21%, decline of 0.1% sequentially," and flagged key H2 margin drivers: "H2 margins will be impacted by compensation hikes, softer revenue seasonality, continued sharing of AI-driven productivity benefits and ramp-up of large deals."

  • Capital return was increased, with Sanghrajka stating: "The Board has announced an interim dividend of INR 26, an increase of 13% compared to last year."

Q&A

  • Kumar Rakesh, BNP Paribas: asked whether Infosys can see next-year organic recovery given the mega deal and AI momentum; CEO Salil Parekh replied, "we feel good that the organic ... will be in a good shape in next year," citing "29% growth quarter-on-quarter" in AI and the mega deal plus pipeline.

  • Kumar Rakesh, BNP Paribas: questioned elevated subcontractor usage and margin impact; CFO Jayesh Sanghrajka said, "there's an endeavor to bring our subcontractor cost down" and added that lowering subcontractors by 1% "gives you around 15 to 20 basis points on margin."

  • Bryan Bergin, TD Cowen: asked what changed most in the growth guidance revision; CFO Sanghrajka pointed to pricing and volumes, saying competitive intensity increased and "that pricing expansion... has not materialized," plus "softer-than-expected" volume and weaker retail/high-tech discretionary demand.

  • Surendra Goyal, Citi: asked about the net-new mega deal’s nature and margin implications; CEO Parekh described "a business transformation opportunity" and said, "We don't see any real margin impact on the transition in this year at all on this one." CFO Sanghrajka added, "there are no asset takeovers. There will be some people takeover."

  • Ankur Rudra, JPMorgan: asked about pricing pressure breadth and H2 assumptions; CEO Parekh said requests are focused on "productivity benefits from the AI that are getting passed on" and CFO Sanghrajka said the low end assumes "similar to slightly deterioration on the pricing" while the high end assumes "improvement."

  • Keith Bachman, BMO: asked if AI is driving more client insourcing and about competitive dynamics; CEO Parekh said, "with AI, we don't see a difference because of AI" on insourcing, and cited higher offshoring and deal selectivity: "we've chosen not to take some deals where the economics didn't make sense."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to pressing on guidance cuts, pricing pressure, vertical weakness (retail/high-tech), and margin durability; TD Cowen directly pressed on what changed in the guide, and JPMorgan asked whether pricing pressure is "broad-based across clients."

  • Management’s tone was slightly positive in prepared remarks and more defensive/qualifying in Q&A; CFO Sanghrajka emphasized uncertainty ranges in the guide, and CEO Parekh repeatedly leaned on AI and deals, saying, "we remain the preferred AI strategy and deployment partner" and "we do remain quite selective in terms of the economics of the contracts."

  • Versus the prior quarter, management sounded more cautious on near-term growth (with the revenue growth range reduced), while continuing to project confidence in AI traction and large-deal conversion; Sanghrajka said, "we are very confident of the guidance that we have given."

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • The FY2027 constant-currency revenue growth range was reduced to "1% to 2%" from the prior quarter’s "1.5% to 3%," while operating margin guidance stayed at "20% to 22%" in both quarters.

  • AI-first revenue mix rose to "10.5% of our revenues" from "8.2%" in the prior quarter, with management emphasizing broader enterprise adoption; Parekh said AI is becoming "central to enterprise transformation" and Sanghrajka said clients are moving to "enterprise-wide adoption."

  • Large deals increased to "$5.2 billion" from "$3.6 billion," and management introduced a net-new "$2 billion-plus 7-year mega deal" expected to contribute "over 1% growth" in FY2028.

  • The prior quarter included a CEO succession announcement; the current quarter did not revisit it in prepared remarks, with focus shifting to guidance revision, AI mix, and mega-deal ramp/transition timing.

Risks and Concerns

  • Sanghrajka cited a cautious demand backdrop: "geopolitical tensions, inflationary pressures and shifting technology priorities" and said "selective discretionary spend" weighed on seasonality.

  • Pricing pressure and competitive intensity were repeated across prepared remarks and Q&A; Parekh said some client demands are "beyond the sort of thresholds of economic return that we are looking at," and Sanghrajka said the low end assumes pricing "deterioration."

  • Margin headwinds were explicitly tied to wage actions and mix/seasonality; Sanghrajka said H2 will be impacted by "compensation hikes" and "continued sharing of AI-driven productivity benefits," partially offset by "Project Maximus."

Final Takeaway

Management emphasized that Q2’s revised FY2027 growth outlook reflects softer-than-expected volumes, pricing pressure, and discretionary caution, while positioning AI-first revenue expansion to 10.5% and $5.2 billion of large deals—including a net-new $2 billion-plus mega deal with an expected FY2028 growth contribution of over 1%—as the main supports for future growth, alongside maintaining the 20% to 22% operating margin framework despite wage and seasonality headwinds.

data.title: First Citizens forecasts $3.5B-$4B quarterly FDIC note prepayments through 2027 as it raises 2026 net interest income to $6.68B-$6.75B
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: First Citizens BancShares (FCNCA) Q3 2026

Management view

  • "Earnings exceeded our expectations during the quarter." (Chairman & CEO Frank Holding) He said results were "headlined by high-quality sequential top line growth" and reported adjusted net income of $652 million and adjusted EPS of $55.37.
  • "Loans were up $6.2 billion over the linked quarter, spearheaded by our premier Fund Banking business." (Chairman & CEO Holding) He also said period-end deposits grew by $11.8 billion and that the BMO branch acquisition added "approximately $4.9 billion in high-quality deposits."
  • "During this quarter, we returned $600 million to shareholders through share repurchases, successfully achieving our target operating range for CET1 capital." (Chairman & CEO Holding) He added the company prepaid "$8 billion of the FDIC purchase money note during the quarter, followed by another $1.5 billion in October."
  • "In the third quarter, adjusted net revenue expanded by 1.4% sequentially, successfully driving positive adjusted operating leverage." (Chief Financial Officer Craig Nix) He said net interest income increased by $43 million linked-quarter and that headline NIM was 3.07%.

Outlook

  • Analysts’ estimates were provided, but the JSON used non-valid quarter formatting (numeric fiscal_quarter rather than Q1-Q4), so comparisons were skipped.
  • "We are raising our fourth quarter loan guidance to a range of $158 billion to $161 billion." (CFO Nix) He said moderation is expected after Q3’s pace: "Following record-breaking production levels year-to-date, we prudently anticipate that balance growth will moderate from the exceptional pace observed in the third quarter."
  • "We project fourth quarter deposits between $189 billion and $192 billion, reflecting a significant increase over our prior guidance." (CFO Nix)
  • "We are raising our full year guidance to $6.68 billion to $6.75 billion, while establishing a fourth quarter range of $1.7 billion to $1.77 billion." (CFO Nix) He said timing effects push some upside into next year: "a meaningful portion of our net interest income upside will materialize as a tailwind in early 2027."

Financial results

  • "We generated adjusted net income of $652 million and adjusted earnings per share of $55.37, driving an ROE of 12.24% and an ROA of 1.08%." (Chairman & CEO Holding)
  • "Lower sequential noninterest income stemmed almost entirely from a $37 million change in warrant income due to valuation adjustments in the current quarter." (CFO Nix) He also highlighted fee drivers including lending-related fees up $10 million and client investment fees up $9 million.
  • "Nonaccrual loans decreased by $80 million sequentially, including the quarter at 0.87% of total loans." (CFO Nix) He said net charge-offs were $103 million and that "we reduced our allowance for loan losses during the quarter."

Q&A

  • Bernard Von Gizycki, Deutsche Bank: asked how asset sensitivity changes with FDIC note paydown; Archibald McClure: "as we look at the alternative funding sources... it should trim a little bit from where we're positioned this quarter." Von Gizycki also asked about M&A; CFO Nix: "We don't have any specific plans currently for whole bank acquisition," but "M&A will remain an important part of our growth strategy."
  • Christopher McGratty, KBW: asked for margin/NII path and betas; CFO Nix: "we expect headline NIM to be in the mid-3.10s" for 4Q’26 exit and for 4Q’27 exit "headline NIM to be in the mid-3.20s"; he added deposit betas "in that 50% range." McGratty also asked about Basel III; CFO Nix said the standardized approach could reduce RWAs "in the mid- to high single digits" and be "accretive to our CET1 ratio by around 70 basis points."
  • Brian Foran, Truist: asked about fund banking pricing and spreads; Elliot Howard: spreads were "largely stabilized" and deposits there are "lower than our average deposits"; another executive added, "compression has slowed" though "competition does remain active." Foran also asked about rate impacts on activity; another executive: "our growth rates are more influenced by fundraising and capital deployment, less so by rate movements alone." Marc Cadieux added the venture pace has been "pretty robust" and enthusiasm "seemingly not diminished" by rates so far.
  • Anthony Elian, JPMorgan: asked about IPO/exits; President of Commercial Banking Marc Cadieux said the IPO bar "remains high" and exit concentration left a "headwind," with secondaries providing some liquidity. Elian also asked about NIM drag from replacement funding; Archibald McClure said replacing the note "will pressure and have a bit of a drag" but called it "more of a temporary drag"; CFO Nix added, "we expect that earning asset yields will outstrip any negative impact of that."
  • Sun Young Lee, TD Cowen: asked if fund banking strength is demand vs. share gains; another executive said, "we are also taking market share" and "booked close to $6 billion in new deals in Q3," while utilization around "40%" may moderate. Lee also asked about reserve levels; CFO Nix: "We're very comfortable where our allowance is right now" and cited coverage of net charge-offs "over 3.4x" quarter-to-date.
  • David Chiaverini, Jefferies: asked about medium-term expenses; Elliot Howard said "low to mid-single digit" is "absolutely fair." Chiaverini also asked about brand alignment; Deanna Hart said feedback has been "really good," and Cadieux added the market sentiment is "name change, whatever" as long as client experience stays the same.
  • Timur Braziler, UBS: asked if margin trajectory holds if FDIC paydown gets more expensive and about cadence; McClure said higher-cost replacement funding is a "known known" but "we do think we have upside" on loan yields; CFO Nix said cadence depends on hike timing and reiterated low single-digit NII growth in 4Q vs. 3Q.
  • Christopher Marinac, Brean: asked about regulatory changes and external opportunities; CFO Nix said proposed changes are "supportive of what we want to do," and Chief Risk Officer Tom Eklund added the environment is "conducive to M&A from a regulatory perspective."

Sentiment analysis

  • Analysts: slightly negative to neutral, repeatedly pressing on FDIC note replacement costs, margin durability, and IPO/liquidity constraints; one example was Anthony Elian’s framing that replacement sources "sound all like more incrementally expensive sources of funding."
  • Management: slightly positive and controlled, emphasizing confidence and mitigation; Archibald McClure acknowledged pressure but said it is "more of a temporary drag," while CFO Nix stated, "our margins will expand."
  • Versus last quarter: management’s tone appeared more confident on balance sheet optimization, shifting from Q2’s paydown pace discussion to Q3’s stated path: "consistent quarterly prepayments in the $3.5 billion to $4 billion range through the end of 2027." (CFO Nix)

Quarter-over-quarter comparison

  • Q3 emphasized larger balance sheet acceleration versus Q2, with loans up $6.2 billion in Q3 (CFO Nix) compared to $2.3 billion in Q2 (CFO Nix), while deposits grew $11.8 billion in Q3 (CFO Nix) versus $2.6 billion in Q2 (CFO Nix).
  • Guidance language moved higher: Q2 guided full-year net interest income of $6.6 billion to $6.75 billion (CFO Nix), while Q3 raised full-year net interest income to $6.68 billion to $6.75 billion (CFO Nix).
  • The FDIC note strategy became more explicit: Q2 described a steady pace of "$500 million to $1 billion per month" (CFO Nix), while Q3 set an end-state timeline: "extinguish the remaining balance in full" by end of 2027 with $3.5 billion to $4 billion quarterly prepayments (CFO Nix).

Risks and concerns

  • "Competition does remain active" in fund finance and spread compression has been a theme, even if management said "compression has slowed." (Unknown Executive)
  • Management acknowledged funding replacement risk: "it will pressure and have a bit of a drag there on the margin component" when replacing the purchase money note with higher-cost channels. (Archibald McClure)
  • Cadieux highlighted exit-market limitations: "the bar remains high for IPOs" and reduced round-trip capital remains a "headwind." (President of Commercial Banking Cadieux)

Final takeaway

Management characterized Q3 as an upside quarter driven by accelerated commercial loan and deposit growth, progress on repaying the FDIC purchase money note, and resilient credit performance. For the next leg, management raised full-year net interest income guidance and increased Q4 balance sheet targets, while laying out a steady quarterly FDIC note prepayment path through 2027, alongside a moderated share repurchase pace now that CET1 is within the target range.

data.title: Balchem signals 22.5%-23% tax rate range while planning new sports partnership announcement
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Balchem (BCPC) Q3 2026

Management View

  • CEO Theodore Harris said the quarter delivered “record quarterly consolidated sales, net earnings and adjusted EBITDA as well as solid cash flows,” citing “healthy broad-based growth across all 3 of our reporting segments” and continued “market penetration of our unique portfolio of specialty nutrients and delivery systems.”

  • CEO Harris highlighted new clinical evidence he said supports Balchem’s branded ingredients, pointing to “encouraging new evidence” from an MD Anderson-led pilot study on choline supplementation in APOE4 carriers and a vitamin K2 study he called “an important, much more significant study, 400 subjects in the study over a longer period of time that really showed cardiovascular benefit of K2.”

  • CFO Carl Bengtsson said profitability improved on mix and manufacturing execution, stating: “Our gross margin as a percentage of net sales expanded 70 basis points to 36.4%. The improvement was driven primarily by higher sales, favorable product mix and manufacturing efficiencies, partially offset by certain higher manufacturing input costs.”

  • CFO Bengtsson framed capital allocation and balance sheet flexibility around buybacks, deleveraging, and capacity for M&A: “We repurchased approximately $28 million of Balchem common stock during the third quarter, and we also reduced net borrowings by $28 million in the quarter, resulting in a net leverage ratio of 0.2x.”

Outlook

  • CFO Bengtsson reiterated typical seasonality and maintained a constructive near-term view: “The fourth quarter for us… is normally sequentially lower than the third quarter based on historic business seasonality, but remain confident in our ability to continue to deliver healthy year-over-year growth in the fourth quarter as we have done all year.”

  • Compared with the prior quarter’s prepared remarks, management again emphasized the same capital priorities—innovation, capacity expansion, and acquisitions—now tying that message to third-quarter leverage of “0.2x” and the “expanded $650 million credit facility we put in place in July.”

  • On tax-rate expectations into year-end, CFO Bengtsson provided a numeric range: “We should be finishing the year in that range of 22.5% to 23%.”

Financial Results

  • The company reported third-quarter consolidated revenue of $291 million and GAAP diluted EPS of $1.46, alongside adjusted diluted EPS of $1.57.

  • CFO Bengtsson reported cash generation and liquidity, saying: “Cash flows from operations were $70 million for the quarter, and free cash flow was $58 million, and we ended the quarter with $66 million of cash on the balance sheet.”

  • Segment performance highlights included Human Nutrition & Health sales of $188 million with earnings from operations of $46 million; Animal Nutrition & Health sales of $63 million with earnings from operations of $6.8 million; and Specialty Products sales of $37 million with earnings from operations of $12 million.

Q&A

  • Bob Labick, CJS Securities, Inc.: asked about margin mix by segment and sustainability; CFO Bengtsson pointed to mix tailwinds, saying nutrition in HNH is “higher margin… and… growing faster than the food part,” and in ANH “the ruminant business… is higher margin than the monogastric and over time is growing faster,” while adding on inflation pass-through: “on a year-to-date basis, we’re pretty much at breakeven.”

  • Bob Labick, CJS Securities, Inc.: asked for next steps on the Alzheimer’s and cardiovascular trials; CEO Harris said the MD Anderson pilot “will lead to a much bigger study,” and for both studies the company will “make sure that our customers are fully aware… and create awareness around studies like this through our marketing efforts.”

  • Daniel Harriman, Sidoti & Company, LLC: asked what’s driving ANH improvement and whether it’s sustainable, plus inventory; CFO Bengtsson cited ruminant penetration and launches (“We just rolled out the next-generation encapsulated methionine actually on October 1”), Europe’s EU antidumping effects with remaining issues (“we still see sort of circumvention happening”), and described inventory at $177 million as driven by “inflationary impact,” growth, “risk mitigation” safety stock tied to “geopolitical situations,” and product-launch build.

  • Raghuram Selvaraju, H.C. Wainwright & Co, LLC, Research Division: asked about future clinical directions (exercise recovery, sleep); CEO Harris pointed to existing and future work, including “studies around muscle recovery,” magnesium science tied to sleep, and additional areas like “beauty from within” and choline benefits “around liver health.”

  • Raghuram Selvaraju, H.C. Wainwright & Co, LLC, Research Division: asked about potential aesthetic partnerships, more sports marketing, oil/fracking impacts, and tax rate; CEO Harris said partnerships in beauty are “a clear opportunity… and something that we are exploring,” and added: “We are contemplating another sports partnership that we should be able to announce… in the next month or so”; CFO Bengtsson said fracking-related choline chloride was “a $5 million business last year” with an “$8 million type of run rate” currently and that “high oil prices is not necessarily a good thing for us,” while reiterating the “22.5% to 23%” effective tax-rate expectation.

  • A question from Artem Chubarov (Rothschild & Company) was attempted, but management said, “we certainly can’t hear him,” and the call ended with no further questions.

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly positive, emphasizing execution and probing sustainability (mix durability, ANH drivers, inventory build), with pointed requests for granularity such as “how sustainable you think it is over time” (Daniel Harriman, Sidoti & Company, LLC).

  • Management’s tone was positive in prepared remarks and remained confident in Q&A, using reinforcing language such as “we remain confident” (CEO Theodore Harris) and “we’re very happy with how ANH has performed” (CFO Carl Bengtsson), while acknowledging ongoing pressures like inflation and EU circumvention.

  • Versus the prior quarter, management again highlighted record performance and consistency, but Q3 added a more explicit commercial/marketing cadence around new published clinical studies and a near-term timing comment on a new sports partnership (“in the next month or so”).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q3 reiterated the same core growth narrative as Q2—“healthy broad-based growth across all 3… segments”—while shifting incremental emphasis from Q2’s capital allocation actions (credit facility expansion and repurchases) to Q3’s clinical publication updates and mix commentary driving margin expansion.

  • Q3 Q&A focused heavily on mix and inventory risk posture, while Q2 Q&A leaned more toward how Balchem selects new nutrients, marketing strategy evolution, and the anticipated publication timing of the MD Anderson pilot study (which Q3 said was published).

  • Management maintained a consistent confidence level quarter-to-quarter, including the continued “consecutive quarter” framing (Q3: “29th consecutive quarter of year-over-year growth in adjusted EBITDA” vs. Q2: “28th consecutive quarter”).

Risks and Concerns

  • CFO Bengtsson flagged inflation pressure and timing effects in pass-through pricing, noting: “We have seen inflation in our raw materials all year. But we have been able to turn around and pass that through to our customers,” while also stating raw-material pass-through can be “a slight negative impact to your margin percentage.”

  • In Europe monogastrics, CFO Bengtsson cited continuing competitive/trade friction: “We still see sort of circumvention happening and absorption where people are just dropping the price to import it and absorbing the duty.”

  • On inventories, CFO Bengtsson tied elevated levels to deliberate safety stock decisions amid “geopolitical situations,” describing it as “from a risk mitigation standpoint.”

Final Takeaway

Balchem’s management emphasized record Q3 results powered by broad-based segment growth, margin support from favorable mix, and strong cash generation that funded both share repurchases and lower borrowings. Executives also elevated the role of newly published clinical studies for VitaCholine and K2VITAL DELTA as near-term marketing catalysts, while acknowledging continued inflation and trade-related headwinds in monogastrics. Looking ahead, management pointed to typical Q4 seasonality but reiterated confidence in year-over-year growth, held its effective tax-rate expectation at 22.5% to 23%, and said it expects to announce another sports partnership “in the next month or so.”

data.title: Rithm outlines $75B-$80B third-party AUM target by end of 2028 while expecting $125M Newrez AI savings
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Rithm Capital Corp. (RITM) Q3 2026

Management View

  • Chairman, President & CEO Michael Nierenberg framed Q3 as resilient amid wider credit and higher rates, saying, "all indices related to markets we invest in were wider. Interest rates rose significantly... and we still had a great quarter," and emphasized the operating platform: "Our operating business lines, Newrez, Genesis performed really well."

  • Nierenberg highlighted servicing scale and the earnings profile of MSRs, noting, "with our MSR business at approximately $880 billion of MSRs at Newrez" and later added, "we don't need to originate a mortgage to make money. If the economics are there, we'll do it. If not, the business performs extremely well and makes a lot of money."

  • On asset management, Nierenberg pointed to fundraising and third-party growth, stating, "Today, we stand at $60-plus billion of third-party AUM," and described the quarter’s progress: "During the quarter, we raised $569 million of new capital... Year-to-date gross inflows are a little bit south of $3 billion."

  • On commercial real estate, Nierenberg reiterated the Elecor/office thesis: "buying office at a 75% discount to replacement value should reward our shareholders well," while Executive VP & Head of Real Estate Peter Brindley said, "We had a great quarter at Elecor Properties," citing leasing and capital markets execution.

  • CFO remarks were not included in this transcript beyond participant introduction; no CFO prepared statement or Q&A answers appeared.

Outlook

  • Nierenberg set an asset-management growth target: "we expect to deliver AUM of about $75 billion to $80 billion by the end of 2028," and said Rithm would also "continue to look at opportunities to grow our asset management business in the M&A world."

  • Management guided to technology-driven cost actions at Newrez, with Nierenberg stating, "We expect to drive going forward, $125 million in savings for Newrez," and Baron Silverstein adding, "We estimate annualized savings from our technology and AI investments of approximately $125 million."

  • On platform timelines, Nierenberg said Valon servicing tech "should come online at the end of Q1 in '27," and Silverstein noted, "phased migration of loans to Valon OS in the first quarter of 2027." Nierenberg also described the earnings ramp: "you'll start to see them kick in, in '27... they'll go on for '27, '28."

  • For Genesis, Nierenberg provided an origination outlook: "I think the production numbers we'll probably do are something between $6 billion and $6.5 billion of production," while emphasizing, "Credit really matters."

Financial Results

  • Nierenberg reported Q3 profitability metrics, stating, "Third quarter EAD of $0.55 per diluted share" and "GAAP net income, $217 million or $0.38 per diluted share," alongside "Earnings available for distribution in the quarter... $315 million."

  • On capital and shareholder distributions, Nierenberg said, "Our common stock dividend... $0.25 per diluted share," and added, "cash and liquidity, we ended the quarter at $1.9 billion," while also noting book value directionally: "we're actually a little bit higher quarter-over-quarter."

  • Segment profitability highlights included Genesis, where Nierenberg stated, "pretax income for the quarter, $33 million" and "the annualized ROE on that business right now is about 13%," and Newrez, where Silverstein said, "third quarter pretax income, excluding mark-to-market of approximately $330 million... delivering a 24% annualized operating ROE."

Q&A

  • Douglas Harter, BTIG: Asked about asset management AUM growth drivers; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg said growth was tied to "big wirehouse banks" distribution and product expansion, adding, "we're seeing extreme demand... in ABF and ABF-type products."

  • Bose George, KBW: Asked if gain-on-sale improvement was mix vs. underlying improvement and about lock trends after rates rose; President Silverstein said, "it definitely is a little bit of a product mix," warned of "more pressure on the wholesale side," and added, "we've seen... a pretty material... decline in production coming from September to October, and you're likely going to see something close to about 25%."

  • Bose George, KBW: Asked about book value quarter-to-date; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg responded, "you should assume it's roughly unchanged."

  • Crispin Love, Piper Sandler: Asked whether infrastructure entry would be small build vs. scaled acquisition; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg said, "it's more likely to be similar to the Sculptor, Crestline or something that's even potentially larger," and emphasized, "it's got to be something of scale."

  • Kenneth Lee, RBC: Asked for Genesis originations outlook given rates; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg said, "$6 billion and $6.5 billion" and added, "The real growth... is going to be more on the multifamily side." Lee also asked what could lift Elecor’s San Francisco occupancy; Executive VP & Head of Real Estate Brindley cited "very manageable lease roll" and said, "we're as active in San Francisco currently as we have been in a very long time."

  • Trevor Cranston, Citizens JMP: Asked about MSR prepay-speed floor and whether servicing plus expense saves can offset origination pressure; President Silverstein said, "I think you're kind of getting to the floor on speeds," adding, "we do think that we have a balanced business model," while Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg pointed to servicing economics, stating, "I think there's roughly $15 billion of escrow deposits" and rate increases are "a huge lift... from a net interest income standpoint."

  • Ameeta Lobo Nelson, UBS: Asked whether investment portfolio focus was growth vs. recycling; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg answered, "I think it's both," and said third-party fee earnings can be prioritized because "Those earnings are recurring and they trade at a much higher multiple." Lobo Nelson also asked about housing policy; President Silverstein said, "We support them," and added, "we'll incorporate that and deliver those savings directly to homeowners."

  • Jason Stewart, Compass Point: Asked about technology positioning; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg said, "our technology budget... is pretty significant" and called Valon "extremely significant," while President Silverstein said, "there is nothing like it in the market." Stewart also asked about liquidity vs. episodic opportunities; Nierenberg said, "we're not here to just grow the balance sheet" and that larger situations will "likely bring in third-party capital."

  • Henry Coffey, Wedbush: Asked if dislocation in commercial/mortgage REITs is an opportunity; Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg said, "we're always looking for opportunities" but added, "We don't want to take over someone else's issues right now." Coffey also asked about correspondent economics in a 7%+ market; Nierenberg said, "we don't need to originate a loan just to have more correspondent value unless we love the valuation of the underlying MSR."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was neutral to slightly skeptical, with questions pressing on origination pressure, MSR floors, infrastructure M&A scale, and capital deployment (e.g., Trevor Cranston asked whether servicing and savings are "enough to offset the pressure on the origination side").

  • Management tone was positive and confident in prepared remarks and mostly steady in Q&A, using definitive framing such as Nierenberg’s "we expect" on savings and AUM targets, and reiterating discipline: "we don't need to originate something for the sake of doing it."

  • Versus last quarter, management kept similar confidence on scaling asset management and technology modernization, but Q3 Q&A carried more explicit discussion of near-term origination volume pressure tied to rates (Silverstein: "material... decline in production") compared with Q2’s more general "higher rates for longer" framing.

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Strategy emphasis stayed consistent: both quarters leaned on platform diversification and third-party AUM growth; Q3 added a specific AUM target (Nierenberg: "$75 billion to $80 billion by the end of 2028") that was not stated in Q2.

  • Technology/AI remained central in both quarters via Valon/HomeVision; Q3 sharpened messaging around savings magnitude ("$125 million") and pushed more of the timing discussion into "'27" and "'28" savings realization.

  • Analyst focus shifted toward rate-driven origination downside and MSR speed floors in Q3, whereas Q2 included more emphasis on capital return questions (buybacks/dividend) that did not recur in Q3.

Risks and Concerns

  • Management highlighted macro and market risks, with Chairman, President & CEO Nierenberg noting, "Interest rates rose significantly, geopolitical concerns persist, oil rose."

  • Origination headwinds from rates were explicit, with President Silverstein citing the "interest rate environment lowering overall origination volumes" and noting a "material... decline in production" moving from September to October.

  • Management flagged competitive pressure and credit-cycle risk, with Silverstein referencing competition "pressure gain on sale margins" and Nierenberg cautioning, "I do think at some point, the credit markets will turn and you start to see delinquencies trend higher."

Final Takeaway

Management described Q3 as another quarter where diversified earnings streams—particularly MSRs and servicing—supported results despite higher rates and wider markets, while reiterating strict origination discipline. Rithm emphasized scaling third-party asset management (including a stated $75B-$80B AUM target by end of 2028), expanding product distribution through large banks, and using technology/AI (including Valon) to pursue $125M of Newrez savings that management expects to materialize through 2027-2028.

data.title: TikTok's U.S. entity seeking four gigawatts of compute power -- CNBC
data.description:
TikTok USDS Joint Venture, the entity that operates the social media platform in the U.S., is attempting to obtain four gigawatts of compute power by early 2030 to run its numerous live machine learning tools, according to sources cited by CNBC.

The company also plans a “flagship B2B AI product at the frontier of large-model inference and creative automation,” according to a job posting. Earlier this year, TikTok USDS Joint Venture also said it was “retraining, testing, and updating” its recommendation algorithm, currently running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure.

TikTok USDS Joint Venture is the entity that was established this year by Silver Lake, Oracle, and MGX to comply with an Executive Order removing China’s ByteDance (BDNCE) as TikTok’s majority owner. Silver Lake, Oracle, and MGX each own a 15% stake in the new entity, while ByteDance holds a 19.9% stake.

Other private investors, including Michael Dell’s family office, own the remaining stake.

data.title: Amerant anticipates $7.3B loans and $8.5B deposits by Q4 2026, while targeting 3.65%-3.70% net interest margin
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Amerant Bancorp (AMTB) Q3 2026

Management View

  • CEO Carlos Iafigliola said Q3 was “another step forward in building a more profitable and resilient franchise,” citing “net income increased to $25.7 million or $0.65 per diluted share, and our return on assets reached 1%,” and attributing the progress to “stronger net interest income and margin expansion, disciplined expense management, continued balance sheet optimization and improving credit quality” (President, CEO & Director Carlos Iafigliola).
  • Iafigliola framed the post-board-strategy priorities as: “deliver on our financial and credit quality commitments, continue simplifying our operating model, focus investment toward the market and capabilities where Amerant has a distinct competitive advantage and deploy capital and resources towards the most attractive opportunities,” while detailing the four initiatives across credit, efficiency, client profitability, and growth (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Iafigliola highlighted deposit mix optimization, saying Amerant “migrated certain low-cost interest-bearing balances to DDAs, which improved our ratio of noninterest-bearing deposits to total deposits without any impact to the retention of these accounts,” alongside “reducing higher cost deposits and selectively exiting nonprofitable single product relationships” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Iafigliola announced a capital return action: “on October 21, our Board authorized a share repurchase program for up to $50 million through December 31, 2027” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • CFO Sharymar Yepez said, “diluted earnings per share for the third quarter was $0.65 per share compared to $0.53 per share in the second quarter,” alongside “net interest margin was 3.77% compared to 3.52% in the second quarter” (Senior EVP & CFO Sharymar Yepez).

Outlook

  • Yepez updated Q4 targets, saying, “we expect total loans to reach approximately $7.3 billion by the fourth quarter of 2026” and “we are revising our total deposit guidance to approximately $8.5 billion by the fourth quarter of 2026” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Yepez guided, “we are revising our expectations for the net interest margin to be in the range of 3.65% to 3.70% in the fourth quarter,” adding, “we expect fourth quarter noninterest expense to be approximately $68 million as we continue making progress toward a target efficiency ratio of approximately 60%” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Compared with Q2 guidance language, management moved from “expect total deposits to reach approximately $9.1 billion by the fourth quarter of 2026” and “expect net interest margin to be approximately 3.50% for the remainder of the year” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez, Q2) to a lower Q4 deposit outlook and a higher but narrower Q4 NIM range (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez, Q3).
  • The analysts estimates JSON included in the prompt used fiscal quarter values that were not in the required Q1–Q4 format, so estimates comparisons were not used.

Financial Results

  • Yepez reported balance sheet shifts: total assets of $10.2 billion (down from $10.3 billion in Q2), cash and cash equivalents of $361.5 million, investment securities of $2.2 billion, gross loans of $7.1 billion, and deposits of $8.2 billion (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Yepez described profitability drivers, reporting net interest income of $90.5 million and noting the margin expansion reflected “a lower cost of funds from noninterest-bearing deposits and shorter-term advances,” plus “additional interest on loan repayments previously in nonaccrual status” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Yepez said credit quality improved, including “nonperforming loans were down $21.6 million or 12.6% to $149.5 million or 1.46% of total assets,” and guided, “we estimate gross charge-offs to be in the range of 30 to 35 basis points for the fourth quarter” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Yepez detailed international deposit composition changes: “deposits from customers domiciled in Venezuela decreased $96.8 million or 3.9%,” while “deposits from countries other than Venezuela increased $87.3 million or 12%” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).

Q&A

  • Michael Rose, Raymond James: asked why Venezuelan deposits fell and how much Q4 deposit growth is international vs. domestic; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola said the decline was “transactional” as reactivation “needed additional CapEx and additional distributions,” and CFO Yepez said Q4 could be “a mix of 60%-40%, 60% coming from the international side and 40% from the domestic side” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola; Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Michael Rose, Raymond James: asked about Q4 margin bridge; Senior EVP & CFO Yepez said Q3 NIM included “collections on loans that were NPL” and after normalizing, “we actually would see some improvement in Q4,” while outlining a modeled December hike scenario tied to “closer to the 3.70%” vs. “closer to the 3.65%” if rates are stable (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Michael Rose, Raymond James: asked “what’s next” after 1% ROA; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola said “the 1% ROA is a new baseline,” and added, “the Amerant of the future should be definitely trying to target the 1.20% in the longer term” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Nicholas Lorenzoni, Stephens: asked if NIB deposit increase was new vs. migrated and sustainability; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola said the change included “approximately $270 million” moved by reclassifying rates to “0,” plus “we were able to grow $100 million into the noninterest-bearing category” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Nicholas Lorenzoni, Stephens: asked about 2027 expenses; Senior EVP & CFO Yepez said early 2027 could be “closer to the $69.5 million to $70 million,” driven by “hiring for growth,” partially offset by “renegotiations of contracts and cost savings initiatives” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Stephen Scouten, Piper Sandler: asked where non-Venezuela international growth came from; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola pointed to “Argentina and other Central American countries” and said the team targets “probably… about 5 countries” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Stephen Scouten, Piper Sandler: asked whether there is an internal cap/regulatory constraint on international deposits; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola said “there is no set cap,” adding “our BSA program… is very consolidated,” and described monitoring concentrations through ALCO (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Stephen Scouten, Piper Sandler: asked about repurchase pace amid ACL/TCE dynamics; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola linked flexibility to the “$50 million blanket until 2027,” and CFO Yepez added, “capital is healthy and provides us the opportunity to balance both growth and the buyback program” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola; Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone was slightly negative to skeptical around deposit volatility and sustainability, with Michael Rose saying he was “a little bit surprised” by Venezuelan deposits and pressing on margin drivers and sensitivity to deposit mix (Michael Rose, Raymond James).
  • Management tone was slightly positive and explanatory, emphasizing confidence and normalization, including “we feel very confident about this growth opportunity” and “the 1% ROA is a new baseline” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez; President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Versus Q2’s tone emphasizing momentum (“momentum remains strong”) and higher year-end deposit guidance, Q3 introduced more qualification around timing (“fluctuation,” “timing of inflows”) and a revised (lower) deposit outlook, while pairing it with stronger profitability metrics and a new buyback authorization (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola; Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • Q3 added a new capital action beyond the ongoing buybacks discussed in Q2: “authorized a share repurchase program for up to $50 million through December 31, 2027” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola).
  • Guidance shifted: Q2 projected Q4 total deposits of $9.1 billion and NIM “approximately 3.50% for the remainder of the year” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez, Q2), while Q3 revised to Q4 deposits “approximately $8.5 billion” and Q4 NIM “3.65% to 3.70%” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez, Q3).
  • The key narrative change on international flows was from Q2’s “Venezuelan deposits increasing close to $500 million from the first quarter” (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola, Q2) to Q3 explaining a Venezuelan decline as “transactional” and pointing to diversification into other countries and wealth management formation (President, CEO & Director Iafigliola; Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).

Risks and Concerns

  • Yepez cautioned that “the interest rate environment will place upward pressure on our cost of funds,” while management positioned mitigants in “repricing of the variable rate loan portfolio,” “deposit repricing discipline,” and “continued growth in lower-cost deposits” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • Management highlighted market-rate risk to capital marks, with Yepez stating, “tangible common equity declined… primarily driven by unrealized losses in the available-for-sale investment portfolio,” while also noting, “the valuation of the AFS portfolio has significantly improved compared to quarter end as market rates have dropped since quarter end” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).
  • On credit, Yepez indicated provisioning reflected “higher specific reserves in the commercial portfolio,” and guided Q4 charge-offs of “30 to 35 basis points,” including “some possible write-offs of existing specific reserves” (Senior EVP & CFO Yepez).

Final Takeaway

Management framed Q3 as a profitability inflection with ROA reaching 1% on higher net interest income and margin expansion, while also emphasizing continued credit clean-up and operating efficiency progress. For Q4, management projected loans of approximately $7.3 billion, revised deposits to approximately $8.5 billion, and guided net interest margin to 3.65%–3.70% amid expected cost-of-funds pressure. Investors also received a new, longer-dated capital return signal with a Board authorization to repurchase up to $50 million of stock through December 31, 2027, alongside ongoing focus on deposit mix optimization and international funding diversification.

data.title: SLB surges on strong Q3 results, upbeat 2027 outlook as Middle East rebounds
data.description:
SLB (SLB) surged 6.5% in Friday's trading after topping Q3 adjusted earnings and revenue estimates while signaling an upbeat 2027 as Middle East activity gradually recovers and Venezuela revenue is expected to more than double.

SLB (SLB) said it has seen a gradual recovery in its Middle East business—the company's biggest ‌market, ⁠accounting for 34% of total revenue in 2025 - despite disruptions from the Iran war, and Q3 revenue from the region rose 13% Q/Q.

The company expects Venezuela to be a "significant growth driver," with revenue on track to more than double by year-end and grow even more in 2027 as international operators ramp up investments, CEO Olivier Le Peuch said during ​the company's earnings conference call.

Overall, Q3 international revenue ticked up 1% to $6.99B, while North American revenue jumped 24% to $2.4B.

Le Peuch said AI demand is driving unprecedented investment in data center infrastructure, and SLB (SLB) is expanding its capabilities to capitalize on the demand, including through its planned $4.1B acquisition of thermal management company Kelvion and the recent buildout of a manufacturing center in Canada.

"We continue to strengthen our position as an industrial technology partner to the data-center industry and to expand our participation in this rapidly growing market," Le Peuch said on the earnings call.

Looking ahead, SLB (SLB) expects global oilfield services activity to grow by a mid-single-digit percentage in 2027, assuming Middle East activity remains at H2 2026 levels and that regional tensions do not escalate further.

data.title: Flagstar forecasts 2027 EPS of $0.85-$0.95 and shifts full turnaround timeline to 2028 amid higher rates
data.description:
Earnings Call Insights: Flagstar Bank (FLG) Q3 2026

Management View

  • "Net interest income increased, the net interest margin expanded and pre-provision net revenue improved compared to the previous quarter," while Flagstar "grew our C&I loan portfolio and deposits while reducing our exposure to commercial real estate loans this quarter" (CEO & Executive Chairman Joseph Otting).
  • "Given a higher for longer interest rate environment, the full realization of our transformation has shifted to 2028 from 2027," and "we are adjusting our guidance" to reflect "higher interest rates," "less deposit growth" and related impacts on "C&I loan growth" and "the net interest margin" (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).
  • "This quarter, we delivered another $2 billion of net C&I loan growth"; CRE payoffs "totaled $1.2 billion"; and Flagstar had "net charge-offs of $74 million or 49 basis points of average loans" (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).
  • "We've adjusted our guidance downward for both '26 and '27, predominantly the result of higher provision costs" tied to NYC rent-regulated multifamily sensitivity to "the forward curve with 4 rate hikes" and "inflationary pressures" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Lee Smith).
  • "We completed the previously approved stock repurchase program of $250 million" ("19.1 million shares" at "approximately $13 per share"), while "total deposits increased about $300 million quarter-over-quarter" and the "CET1 ratio" was "12.38%" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • "During the third quarter, we generated $4.6 billion in new and increased C&I loan commitments" and "C&I loans during the third quarter increased $2 billion to $20.6 billion"; Flagstar also had a "strong pipeline going into the fourth quarter at $2.7 billion" (Chief Banking Officer, Co-President & Co-COO Richard Raffetto).

Outlook

  • No usable analysts-estimates comparison was included because the provided estimates used an invalid fiscal-quarter format.
  • "EPS for '26 is now forecast to be in the $0.10 to $0.15 range and EPS for '27 is forecast to be in the $0.85 to $0.95 range"; Flagstar added a new view that "EPS is expected to be $1.60 to $1.70" in 2028 (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • "We expect the balance sheet to grow on average approximately $1 billion a quarter in 2027 and 2028," driven by "net new loan growth of $2 billion" with funding split "approximately 50% with deposit growth and 50% with CRE runoff" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • Management framed 2027 as an inflection driven by contractual repricing: "between October 1, 2026, and December 31, '27, we have $12 billion of low coupon, less than 3.9% CRE multifamily loans either resetting or maturing" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).

Financial Results

  • "Our NIM expanded 4 basis points in Q3 versus Q2 to 2.17%, with the September NIM coming in at 2.23%" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • "We generated plus $0.13 of earnings" pre-credit provision in Q3, which "included a $22 million or $0.04 tax benefit" from settling "a legacy tax audit from 2020" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • "We still expect full year '26 operating expenses to decline approximately $168 million or 9% year-over-year versus full year 2025" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • Credit metrics and reserves discussed on the call included: "an increase in our provision expense to $76 million in the third quarter"; "nonaccrual loans were relatively stable" at "approximately $2.8 billion"; and "criticized and classified loans increased $670 million or 6%" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).

Q&A

  • Christopher McGratty, KBW: Asked about reset/maturity visibility; CFO Smith: "2027 is our biggest reset and maturity year" and migration was "very formulaic" using DSCR, with "the vast majority of the migration this quarter" on market units.
  • Christopher McGratty, KBW: Asked about buybacks given CET1 vs. target; CEO Otting: "don't envisage us doing any additional stock buybacks in the fourth quarter" and "would expect to resume buybacks in 2027."
  • David Rochester, Cantor Fitzgerald: Asked about deposit capture from C&I; CBO Raffetto: Flagstar brought "just under $600 million of deposits" on "$2 billion" net C&I growth, and "we feel pretty good about bringing in 30% of deposits."
  • David Rochester, Cantor Fitzgerald: Asked about confidence in 2028 ramp; CFO Smith: said the company added bridge slides because key drivers are "balance sheet growth" and "fixed asset repricing," while deposit assumptions were detailed, including new deposit cost assumptions of "between 3.9% and 4%."
  • David Chiaverini, Jefferies: Asked what is most at risk in NII drivers; CFO Smith: deposit growth is the key question—"can we deliver on the deposit growth"—while repricing is "all mechanical."
  • Casey Haire: Asked about net charge-offs guide and deposit beta; CFO Smith: "I would look at that as the proxy for net charge-offs" (provision forecast), and deposit beta targeting included "we are targeting a 60% beta."
  • Jared Shaw, Barclays: Asked about growth assumptions and rent-reg landlord sentiment; CFO Smith: growth is "predicated on the deposit" and "90% of the growth is going to come from C&I"; CEO Otting: borrowers may want "the bank to restructure and lower their interest rate off the contractual coupon."
  • David Smith, Truist: Asked for ending assets; CFO Smith: "end of '26... $82.1 billion" and "end of '27, $92.1 billion... end of '28... around $97 billion."
  • Ryan Kenny, Morgan Stanley: Asked about noninterest-bearing deposit growth; CFO Smith: the shift reflected reclassifying "$900 million to $1 billion" of very low-rate interest-bearing accounts to noninterest-bearing.
  • Ebrahim Poonawala, BofA: Pressed on suspending buybacks; CEO Otting: "it's prudent until we build our core earnings and ensure that our credit quality forecast is accurate"; on M&A, CEO Otting: "we think the best value... is for us to execute on our business plan."
  • Benjamin Gerlinger, Citigroup: Asked curve timing and rate sensitivity; CFO Smith: forecast used "a September curve that had 4 hikes" and added, "If rates come down, that is definitely beneficial" for credit.
  • Anthony Elian, JPMorgan: Asked about selling rent-regulated exposure; CEO Otting: "we have currently like nothing on the table to do that" and said internal resolutions have been "with 1% to 5%" near marks while investors target "15% to 20% returns."

Sentiment Analysis

  • Analysts’ tone skewed slightly negative and pressing around buybacks, rate sensitivity, and rent-regulated exposure, including "why are we shutting down the buybacks?" and whether the franchise is "very much an interest rate curve bet" (Ebrahim Poonawala, BofA Securities; Benjamin Gerlinger, Citigroup).
  • Management tone in prepared remarks was slightly positive on execution but tempered on timing, with CEO Otting saying the 2028 shift was "a change in timing, not in our strategy nor expectations," while Q&A included caution such as "it's prudent" to pause buybacks until credit and earnings visibility improve (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).
  • Versus the prior quarter’s prepared confidence ("we are confident that we are on the right path"), the current call used more timing-and-macro framing ("higher for longer") and explicitly extended the turnaround timeline (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).

Quarter-over-Quarter Comparison

  • In Q2, Flagstar announced "a $250 million share buyback" (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting); in Q3, management said it "completed" that program but "don't envisage" additional buybacks in Q4, with an expectation to "resume" in 2027 (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).
  • Guidance language shifted materially: Q2 said "EPS for '26... $0.40 to $0.50" and "EPS for '27... $1.60 to $1.70" (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith); Q3 reset to "$0.10 to $0.15" for 2026 and "$0.85 to $0.95" for 2027, while adding 2028 EPS guidance (CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).
  • Strategy emphasis remained centered on C&I growth and CRE reduction, but Q3 added explicit timing slippage: "full realization of our transformation has shifted to 2028 from 2027" (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).
  • Analyst focus broadened from Q2’s buyback authorization and NIM trajectory to Q3’s higher-rate credit implications, deposit competitiveness, and whether portfolio sales or strategic combinations were being considered.

Risks and Concerns

  • Management tied higher credit costs to "higher interest rates," "actions related to the New York City rent regulations" and "persistent inflationary pressures," while also citing "a competitive deposit environment" as a constraint (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting).
  • CFO Smith described a rate/inflation transmission into rent-regulated multifamily via "increased cap rates," "put pressure on debt service coverage ratios," and "increased the risk that more loans migrate to criticized and classified status," and linked this to higher provisioning.
  • On mitigation, management emphasized mechanical repricing and remixing: resets/maturities are "all contractual," and the plan relies on "reduce our New York rent-regulated exposure" and fund C&I growth with deposits plus CRE runoff (CEO & Executive Chairman Otting; CFO, Co-President & Co-COO Smith).

Final Takeaway

Management presented Q3 as continued operational progress—C&I growth, CRE runoff, and modest NIM improvement—but reset the investment narrative around a “higher for longer” rate backdrop that raised provision expense, tightened deposit-growth assumptions, and pushed “peer-like metrics” timing out by roughly a year. The updated earnings path centered on contractual CRE repricing and planned balance-sheet growth funded half by deposits and half by CRE runoff, while capital return shifted from completing the prior $250M program to pausing further buybacks in Q4 and pointing to a 2027 resumption tied to core earnings and credit visibility.
